title: Drip Drop
author: Yashaswini A Singh
body:
Drip-drop and then a few more drops.
All move out, silence is just ringing now.
Awakening the voices,
whispering through their creepy laughter:

“How was the trip?”
“Did you fall again?”
“What was it this time?”
“Did you get shut out or was it you being too much?”

“First problem was your skills,
then the problem was you
and now the problem was your mouth!!?”
“Really this fate of your is just too hilarious!”
“Hahahaha!”

It is like a story being sold
Yourself being exposed
This loneliness has now become comforting and nice
Scary at the plead, then conlding your mind

This is a loop, that keeps make up,
makes you feel like you had enough
This is the feeling of my noisy mind,
this is also me with nothing on my mind.

title: This is how it feels
author: Sanjana
body:
I have been waiting for the curtain to drop since I can recall. Of all the materials in the world, I despise latex the most, because my costume is made out of it. It sticks to the skin like it wants to replace it. I am partially latex now and the conjunctions of the latex and my skin are sewn together.

It matters how I cry and I wish it didn’t. I wish it didn’t feel like everybody is watching how tears roll down my cheeks and whether the redness of my eyes matches the intensity of my grief. Birds sleep, but they lie awake, their prying eyes ready to find fallacies in my being, in my aloneness, in my crisis.

It's easy to let them look at my happiness even if they do so with doubt, but it's been tiring to perform through breakdowns. They care too much to let me be in solidarity but too little to offer help.

They notice how I hold my own hair back as I throw up the food down the sink. They notice how my hands are used to it. They notice and they murmur. I play music loud enough to mute their criticism, but lately they have started chanting it like a holy ritual. When I cut, they nod in disapproval when it doesn’t leave scars.

I wish they would see that my feet can’t bear my weight anymore because the food I eat is the food I throw out, hot five minutes later with two fingers down my throat. When I panic away on the grave of the bed, they watch. They watch as I struggle to breathe and ugly cry, they take down their notepads and score me for it. The distance between their panel and my stage is not that much, can’t they see that? I screamed for their help and I begged them to let me stop performing. They sharpen the spotlight in response. The next time I open my eyes, I see a thousand pairs of theirs, around my bed, some behind the headboard. They are curious as I wither away, they want to see a stage girl decompose on the stage.

I pull at the stitches to undo the costume from my skin, but parts of my skin come off instead. There is so much blood on the floor now that it reminds me that my insides are submerged in it, that underneath all the stitches, there is blood that they haven’t touched yet. There are parts that have not been felt up, that my insides are mine alone. They chant louder and the chants say that I seek attention. I find it hypocritical, so I laugh. They judge my laughter because it's crooked.

I have no fear of dying. I just don’t want to die where I was confined to all my life. I want my death to be meaningless and unevaluated. For my last act, I want them to stop looking.

title: where
author: Vidhi Kataria
body:
where does a poet go,

when he no longer is able to write?

where does a poet go,

when his poems no longer make sense?

where does a poet go,

when his muse no longer inspires him?

where does a poet go,

when his hands fear his thoughts?

where does a poet go,

when his pen runs out of ink?

where does a poet go,

when there is no paper left?

where does a poet go,

when there is no light, no day?

where does a poet go,

when his feelings start speaking-

a language so foreign, that even,

his heart can no longer understand?

where does a poet go,

when everything around him,

moves with the speed of light?

almost as if, the light is running away,

no longer wanting to cut through the

darkness that lay beneath all his words

tell me, where does a poet go,

when he no longer wishes to write?

title: The Cartographer of Forgotten Rooms
body:
Professor Ghosh had a peculiar hobby: he drew maps of rooms that no longer existed. Not famous rooms — not the library of Alexandria or the war room at Bletchley Park — but ordinary rooms. His grandmother's kitchen. The classroom where he first understood calculus. The hospital room where his daughter was born.

He worked from memory, which meant each map was slightly wrong. The kitchen was always larger than it had been. The classroom had windows it never possessed. The hospital room faced a garden that existed only in his grief.

"Memory is a terrible cartographer," he would tell his students. "It moves walls, adds doors, changes the light. But it never loses the feeling of a room. The dimensions lie. The atmosphere is always true."

When he died, his daughter found forty-seven maps in his desk drawer. She couldn't identify a single room. But standing in her own kitchen, holding the papers that smelled of his pipe smoke, she understood every one of them.

title: Storming the Mind's Bastion
author: Kedhar Vinod
body:
A sudden storm raging on the front door,
Breaking the security present,
To let itself into the room of control,
Leaving it breached and vulnerable to attacks once again.

Footprints that moved with precision, falter along the same route,
Moving, more like stumbling down the fogged path,
A warning siren blaring through the chest,
Warning the impending attack on itself

The pounding of the heart increasing,
Like a prisoner, attempting to escape captivity
Hands turning cold and stone
Eyes fluttering between the silhouette of reality,
And cold and hypnotising darkness

All routes to regain normalcy,
Being intercepted, ambushed from every side,
Breaths turning into pockets of hope,
Consciousness and subconscious, uniting for a war against the unconscious

With no lifelines present nearby,
Or a branch of reality to cling onto,
The soldiers fight a losing war against the oppressor,
Causing the body to wriggle in agony to the foreseeable future,

Its screams voiceless and captured,
Limbs turning into stone at every passing moment,
While the war is still being waged,
With no retreat being passed by the oppressor

Each remaining resource of the defenders,
Being trampled and trodden by the powerful forces of the attackers,
Conceding to the capture of the head,
And thereby shutting its operations while the attempt to restart continues.

Silently but surely,
Awakening the last attempt,
To overturn the written decree,
And regain control and functioning
"And in the silence that followed, I wondered,
Was it ever under my control at all?"

title: The Lending Library of Last Resort
body:
The rules of the Lending Library of Last Resort were simple: you could borrow any book, but you had to leave one behind. Not just any book — the book that had changed your life the most. The one you'd read so many times the spine cracked when you opened it to your favorite page.

Most people hesitated at the threshold. Some turned back entirely. But those who entered found shelves lined with the most extraordinary collection in the world — not rare first editions or ancient manuscripts, but paperbacks with broken spines and dog-eared pages, highlighted passages and tear-stained chapters. Books that had been loved so hard they were falling apart.

The librarian, a woman whose age was as indeterminate as the library's location, never recommended books. She simply watched which shelf your hand reached for first. "That's the one," she'd say, before you even pulled it free. She was never wrong.

I left behind my copy of 'Letters to a Young Poet.' I took home someone's battered 'Kitchen' by Banana Yoshimoto. Inside the cover, in handwriting I'll never identify, someone had written: 'This book taught me that grief and hunger are the same thing.' I've been thinking about that sentence for three years. I think I'm beginning to understand.

title: A heart that didn't learn
author: Liyana AM
body:
After all this time, My heart still knows your name,
Yet I'm the only one there is left to blame.
Maybe you never meant to leave my life,
But my friends tell me that's a lie.

I look around and see everything that reminds me of you,
Would your surroundings have reminded you of me too?
I sit in the empty room, wondering when I will let go of your hand,
Things definitely didn't go as planned.

I still remember when you called me biscuit,
I wish I could go back just to relive it.
For all I do is yearn ,
As my heart remains a heart that didn't learn.

title: THE WEIGHT OF FEELING
author: Riya Kendadath
body:
The mirror looks on
A hesitant expression , guarded connections
It's the same as it was before
Yet very different

Bade farewell to inner turmoil ,
Gave in to the numbness
As it envelops the whole self ,
And becomes a way of life

Wonderment ceases when it diverges to
Overthinking
Feeling too much is a curse
But what about feeling too little ?

What about going from feeling too much to making oneself feel too little ?
Coping is surviving
With that one moves on and tries not to look back
For looking back brings back memories and nostalgia

And feeling too little doesn't seem bad
The self is stuck nevertheless
It's an never-ending loop
Added with progress

Enchanted to feel alive now
But for how long?
How long until it starts again ?
And the mind rises in an usurper once again
And maybe the truce is a delusion

And maybe It's an olive branch being extended
For prowess in resilience ,
Accepted by a self still
Learning how to breathe.

Uncertainty is inevitable
And embracing it
by yielding to its tide
Becomes a shield.

The loop may persist
But so does the strength
And I've learned to anchor the storm now.
Fear may eventually be overpowered
And inner trust reflects in guarded eyes.
